cards.back: Upper: nose/mouth to larynx (vocal cords). Lower: below the larynx - trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.
Leaf-shaped flap that covers the glottis during swallowing to keep food and fluid out of the trachea.
Firm ring at the lower larynx; the only complete cartilage ring of the airway. Site of cricoid pressure (Sellick), which is no longer routinely recommended.
Adam's apple; shield-shaped, largest laryngeal cartilage, protects the vocal cords.
Point where the trachea divides into the right and left mainstem bronchi.

cards.front: Why is the right mainstem bronchus more prone to foreign bodies/intubation errors?
cards.back: It is shorter, wider and straighter (less angled) than the left.
Tiny air sacs where O2 and CO2 are exchanged with pulmonary capillary blood by diffusion.
Main muscle of inspiration. Contracts and flattens, increasing chest volume and lowering pressure so air flows in.
Inhalation is active: diaphragm and intercostals contract. Exhalation is passive: muscles relax, chest recoils.

cards.front: Normal room air O2 and CO2 composition
cards.back: About 21% oxygen, 78% nitrogen, ~0.04% CO2. Exhaled air is ~16% oxygen (enough for rescue breaths).

cards.front: Primary stimulus to breathe in healthy people
cards.back: Rising CO2 in the blood/CSF (hypercarbia), sensed by chemoreceptors in the medulla. Low O2 (hypoxic drive) is the backup stimulus.
In chronic CO2 retainers (some COPD), low O2 becomes the breathing stimulus. Never withhold O2 from a hypoxic patient.
Ventilation: movement of air in and out of the lungs. Respiration: gas exchange (O2/CO2) at alveoli and cells.
Volume of one normal breath, about 500 mL (5-7 mL/kg).
Tidal volume x respiratory rate; air moved per minute.
Airway volume not involved in gas exchange (~150 mL in adults): trachea, bronchi, mouth, nose.
12-20 breaths/min.

cards.front: Normal child respiratory rates by age (approx)
cards.back: Toddler 24-40; preschool 22-34; school-age 18-30; adolescent 12-20 breaths/min. Ranges vary slightly by textbook.
About 30-60 breaths/min (newborn 40-60; slows toward 30-50 by 1 year).
About 95-100% on room air. Below 94% suggests hypoxia; treat the patient, not the number alone.
Falsely high with carbon monoxide (reads COHb as oxyHb); unreliable with poor perfusion, cold extremities, nail polish, motion.
Rate within normal range, regular rhythm, equal chest rise, clear equal breath sounds, good skin color, normal effort.
Abnormal rate/rhythm, shallow or unequal rise, cyanosis, retractions, nasal flaring, accessory muscle use, tripod, altered mentation.
Anxiety, restlessness, tachypnea, tripod, accessory muscle use, ability to speak only in short phrases.
Slow or irregular rate, fatigue, decreased LOC, weak cry, cyanosis, bradycardia in children. Needs assisted ventilation.
Skin pulling in at the ribs, above clavicles or sternum during inhalation; sign of increased work of breathing (esp. children).
Blue-gray skin/mucous membranes from low O2 in blood; late sign of hypoxia.
Signs of respiratory distress in infants and children; seesaw breathing (abdominal) is also seen.
Sitting upright leaning forward on hands; sign of significant respiratory distress.
35-45 mmHg. Waveform also shows bronchospasm (shark fin) and CPR quality. Monitoring use at EMT level is per local protocol.
High-pitched whistling, usually on exhalation; narrowed lower airways (asthma, COPD, anaphylaxis).
Harsh, high-pitched crowing sound on inhalation; upper airway obstruction (croup, epiglottitis, foreign body, swelling).
Low-pitched, rattling/snoring sounds; secretions in larger airways (bronchitis, pneumonia).
Fine bubbling or crackling on inspiration; fluid in alveoli (CHF/pulmonary edema, pneumonia).
Fluid (blood, vomit, secretions) in the upper airway. Suction immediately.
Partial obstruction by tongue or soft tissue in an unresponsive patient. Open the airway, consider an adjunct.
Collapsed lung, pneumothorax, hemothorax, severe asthma 'silent chest', airway obstruction.
Both sides, comparing left to right: apices (below clavicles, midclavicular), midaxillary, and bases (posterior lower back).
Gradual increase then decrease in rate/depth with periods of apnea; seen with brain injury, stroke, CHF, end of life.
Deep, rapid, labored breathing; blowing off CO2 to compensate for metabolic acidosis (DKA).
Irregular pattern with unpredictable pauses; sign of increased ICP / brainstem damage.
Occasional gasping, slow and ineffective breaths near death; NOT adequate breathing. Treat as arrest and start CPR.
Deep, rapid, regular breathing from brainstem injury.
Prolonged inspiratory gasp with pause; brainstem (pons) damage.
Fast rate / slow rate / absent breathing.
Rate/depth too much, blowing off CO2 / too little, retaining CO2. Hypoventilation needs ventilation assistance.
Ketones: diabetic ketoacidosis (often with Kussmaul breathing).
Chest segment moves opposite to the rest of the chest; flail chest (2+ adjacent ribs broken in 2+ places).
Insufficient oxygen at the tissue level. Signs: restlessness, tachycardia, cyanosis, altered mental status.
Too much CO2 in the blood; drowsiness, headache, flushed skin, from hypoventilation.

cards.front: Early vs late signs of hypoxia
cards.back: Early: anxiety, restlessness, tachycardia, tachypnea. Late: cyanosis, confusion, decreased LOC, bradycardia (especially in children).
Air under the skin that crackles like bubble wrap; suggests pneumothorax/airway or chest injury.

cards.front: Jugular vein distention and tracheal deviation
cards.back: Tension pneumothorax: JVD and tracheal deviation (a late, often absent sign) with hypotension and absent breath sounds on the affected side.
Drop in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inhalation; seen in severe asthma, tamponade.
Alert, Verbal, Painful, Unresponsive; level of consciousness guides airway risk. Opening airways often needed at P or U.

cards.front: Agonal gasps or brief seizure-like activity in a collapsed patient
cards.back: May be the onset of cardiac arrest. Check pulse and breathing together for no more than 10 sec; if no pulse or unsure, start CPR.
Opens the airway when no spinal injury is suspected: tilt the head back and lift the chin to move the tongue off the posterior pharynx.
Airway maneuver for suspected spinal injury; push mandible forward from the angles of the jaw.

cards.front: Modified jaw thrust when it fails
cards.back: If the jaw thrust fails to open the airway in trauma, use head-tilt chin-lift; airway takes priority over spine.
Unresponsive patient with no gag reflex. Keeps the tongue from obstructing the airway; still requires proper head position.
Responsive patient or any patient with a gag reflex; may cause vomiting or laryngospasm.
Measure from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or angle of the jaw (some texts: center of mouth to angle of jaw).
Insert upside down and rotate 180 degrees at the soft palate, or use a tongue depressor and insert right-side up. Children: tongue depressor, no 180 rotation.
Semiconscious or unresponsive patients who have a gag reflex or clenched jaw and cannot keep their own airway (e.g., seizure, AMS).
Suspected basilar skull fracture or severe facial/nasal trauma, or nasal obstruction. Stop if resistance is met. Per local protocol.
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe; diameter about the size of the patient's little finger or nostril.
Lubricate (water-soluble), bevel toward the septum, advance along the floor of the nose, usually right nostril; if resistance, try the other side.
For unresponsive patients breathing adequately with a pulse and no suspected spinal injury; lets fluids drain to limit aspiration.
Unit should generate at least 300 mmHg of vacuum with the tubing clamped. Limit each adult suction attempt to about 15 sec (10 sec per some protocols).
Adult up to 15 sec, child up to 10 sec, infant up to 5 sec per attempt (some protocols: 10 sec for all). Oxygenate/ventilate before and after.
Use lower vacuum than adults: commonly about 80-120 mmHg for children and under 100 mmHg for infants. Exact figures per local protocol.
Used for mouth and pharynx to remove large particles, blood, vomit; insert only as far as can be seen.
Flexible catheter for the nose, a stoma/tracheostomy tube, or liquid secretions when a rigid tip won't fit; measure nose tip to earlobe.

cards.front: Vomiting patient with suspected spinal injury
cards.back: Log roll the patient as a unit onto the side while maintaining spinal alignment, then suction the airway.
Good air exchange, able to cough forcefully and speak. Encourage coughing, do not interfere, and monitor for worsening.
Cannot speak, cough or breathe. 2025 AHA: cycles of 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts until cleared. If unresponsive, start CPR.
2025 AHA: cycles of 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts (heel of one hand), head lower than body. No abdominal thrusts. If unresponsive, start CPR.
Use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts (late pregnancy, or when you cannot encircle the abdomen).
Slight neck flexion with head extension to align the airway in adults and older children. Infants: neutral position (pad under shoulders).
Ventilate through the stoma using an infant/child mask sealed around it; no head tilt needed. If air leaks from mouth/nose, seal them. Suction as needed.
Suction the tube first. If still obstructed, follow protocol (e.g., remove/clean inner cannula); ventilate via the tube or stoma with a BVM.
Not in the national EMT scope of practice (AEMT and above). Some states/agencies allow EMTs to insert them with extra training per local protocol.
A collar must not impair breathing or airway access; keep manual stabilization and use jaw thrust if the airway needs opening.

cards.front: Foreign body removal in unresponsive patient
cards.back: Start CPR. Each time you open the airway to ventilate, look in the mouth and remove an object only if visible. No blind finger sweeps.

name: NREMT · Oxygen, BVM, CPAP & Respiratory Conditions

cards.front: Nonrebreather mask flow rate and FiO2
cards.back: 10-15 L/min, enough to keep the reservoir inflated; delivers up to about 90% oxygen (less in practice with a poor mask seal).

cards.front: Nasal cannula flow rate and FiO2
cards.back: 1-6 L/min; delivers about 24-44% oxygen (approx. 4% per liter).
6-10 L/min; approximately 35-60% oxygen. Never run below 6 L/min (CO2 rebreathing).
Delivers a fixed, precise FiO2 (about 24-50%) set by a color-coded adapter; useful when controlled oxygen is needed (e.g., COPD).
6-10 L/min with reservoir, no one-way valves; about 35-60% oxygen. Rarely used in the field.
For infants/children who won't tolerate a mask: hold tubing, mask or cup near the face at 6 L/min or more (flow per local protocol).
Minutes = (gauge psi - safe residual) x cylinder constant / flow in L/min. Constants: D 0.16, E 0.28, M 1.56, G 2.41, H/K 3.14.
200 psi is the textbook value used in duration calculations; many services change tanks at 500 psi. Follow local policy.

cards.front: Full pressure of an oxygen cylinder
cards.back: About 2,000 psi (2,000-2,200 psi) when full.
Keep away from heat, flame, oil and grease; secure cylinders; open the valve slowly. Oxygen is a drug and supports combustion (it does not burn itself).
Hypoxia (SpO2 <94%), respiratory distress, shock, CO poisoning, cardiac arrest. Chest pain/stroke: only if hypoxic or dyspneic. Titrate per protocol.
No absolute contraindication in a hypoxic patient. Avoid routine high-flow O2 when SpO2 is normal (e.g., uncomplicated MI or stroke).
Adult with a pulse but inadequate breathing: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min), each over about 1 sec, just enough for chest rise.

cards.front: BVM ventilation rate - child and infant
cards.back: With a pulse: 1 breath every 2-3 seconds (20-30/min) per AHA (2020 and 2025). Older texts/some protocols list 12-20/min.
Just enough to produce visible chest rise (about 500-600 mL in adults). Avoid excessive rate/volume: gastric distention, reduced cardiac output.
One rescuer holds the mask seal with two hands and opens the airway; the other squeezes the bag. Preferred over one-person BVM.
Thumb and index finger form a C on the mask; remaining 3 fingers form an E along the jaw.
With a reservoir and 15 L/min oxygen: about 90-100%. With oxygen but no reservoir: about 40-60%. Room air only: 21%.
Air in the stomach from too much volume, force or rate; causes vomiting and limits lung expansion. Reposition airway; give slow, gentle breaths.
Awake patient able to follow commands with moderate-severe respiratory distress (pulmonary edema/CHF, COPD, asthma per protocol) and adequate BP.
Apnea/agonal breathing, unresponsive or unable to protect airway, vomiting/GI bleed, hypotension (SBP <90), pneumothorax or chest trauma, facial trauma.
Continuous positive airway pressure keeps alveoli open, pushes fluid out of lungs, increases oxygenation and reduces work of breathing.
Reversible bronchospasm, swelling and mucus with wheezing. Oxygen if hypoxic, position of comfort, assist prescribed inhaler/albuterol per protocol.
Chronic airflow limitation; wheezes/rhonchi, barrel chest, pursed lips. Titrate O2 (commonly SpO2 88-92% per protocol); never withhold if hypoxic.
Exhaling slowly through pursed lips creates back-pressure that keeps small airways open (self-made PEEP); common in COPD/emphysema.
Beta-2 agonist bronchodilator. EMTs assist with the patient's prescribed inhaler or give it per protocol. Side effects: tachycardia, tremor, nervousness.
Check right drug/expiration, shake, exhale, seal lips (use spacer if available), press while inhaling slowly and deeply, hold breath about 10 sec.
Lung infection: fever, productive cough, crackles/rhonchi, pleuritic pain. O2 if hypoxic, position of comfort, monitor, transport.
Clot blocks a pulmonary artery: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia. Risks: immobility, surgery, estrogen. O2, rapid transport.
Air in the pleural space without trauma (classically tall, thin young males, smokers, COPD); sudden sharp pain, dyspnea, decreased sounds one side.
Trapped pleural air collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum: severe distress, absent sounds, hypotension, JVD. Needs ALS decompression; rapid transport.
Seal with a vented chest seal or occlusive dressing (3-sided taping per local protocol). If tension signs develop, lift/burp the dressing.
Fluid in alveoli (usually left heart failure): crackles, pink frothy sputum, orthopnea. Sit upright, O2, CPAP if indicated per protocol.
Croup: viral, barking cough, stridor, age ~6 mo-3 yr. Epiglottitis: high fever, drooling, tripod; keep calm, nothing in the mouth, no throat exam.
Stridor, wheezing, hoarseness, swelling of lips/tongue/throat. Give epinephrine (auto-injector/IM) per protocol first; O2 and airway support.
Rapid breathing with tingling, carpopedal spasm, dizziness. Calm and coach; no paper bag. Assume a serious cause (PE, DKA, MI) until ruled out.
Relatively larger tongue in a smaller mouth; more likely to block the airway.
Narrower and more easily blocked by swelling, mucus, or blood; small edema causes large resistance.
Softer, shorter and more flexible; hyperextension or flexion can kink it. Keep infants neutral and children in a slight sniffing position.
Classically taught as the narrowest part of the airway in children under about 8-10 years (in adults it is the glottis/vocal cords).
Young infants (first months of life) breathe mainly through the nose; nasal secretions can cause distress. Clear nostrils with a bulb syringe.
Large occiput flexes the neck when supine; place a folded towel under the shoulders of an infant/young child to keep the airway neutral.
Soft and pliable; children rely on the diaphragm (belly breathing). Retractions and seesaw breathing signal increased work of breathing.
Higher metabolic rate and smaller reserves, so they desaturate quickly. Respiratory failure/hypoxia is the most common cause of pediatric arrest.
Bradycardia in a hypoxic child signals impending arrest. Ventilate with O2; if HR stays <60 with poor perfusion, start compressions.
Size corner of mouth to earlobe/angle of jaw. Insert right side up using a tongue depressor; do not rotate 180 degrees (palate injury).
Size carefully (nose tip to earlobe, smaller than the nostril). Small passages bleed and block easily; rarely used in infants. Per local protocol.
About 100-160 bpm (newborns may reach 180). Ranges vary slightly by textbook.
Approx: toddler 90-150, preschool 80-140, school age 70-120, adolescent 60-100 bpm. Ranges vary by source.

cards.front: Pediatric hypotension: lowest acceptable systolic BP
cards.back: Ages 1-10: below 70 + (2 x age in years) mmHg is hypotension. Over 10 years: <90. Infants 1-12 mo: <70; newborns: <60.
Appearance, Work of breathing, Circulation to skin. Quick general impression.

cards.front: Pediatric respiratory arrest vs cardiac arrest
cards.back: Most pediatric arrests are respiratory in origin; prioritize airway and ventilation.
Severe, responsive: child gets 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts (2025 AHA); infant gets 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts. Unresponsive: CPR.
Child up to 10 sec, infant up to 5 sec per attempt, with lower vacuum; avoid deep or prolonged suction (vagal bradycardia, hypoxia).
Mask should cover from the bridge of the nose to the chin cleft without pressing on the eyes; don't compress soft tissue under the chin.
Infant: under 1 year. Child: 1 year to puberty. Adult: puberty and older (breast development in females; chest/underarm hair in males).
Common with excessive force, volume or rate; it pushes up the diaphragm. Give gentle breaths over 1 sec, just enough for chest rise.

cards.front: Febrile child with drooling and tripod
cards.back: Suspect epiglottitis: keep calm, position of comfort, nothing in the mouth, no throat exam, blow-by O2 if tolerated, rapid quiet transport.
Viral infection of small airways in infants/toddlers: wheezing, nasal flaring, retractions. Suction the nose, give oxygen as needed.
Wheezing, retractions, and tiring child; silent chest is critical. Assist with prescribed inhaler per protocol.

cards.front: Altered mental status in a child: what to check
cards.back: Hypoxia first (airway/breathing), then blood glucose; hypoglycemia is common in sick children and causes lethargy or seizures.
Neutral position; flexion or hyperextension can kink the soft airway. A thin pad under the shoulders offsets the large occiput.
SIDS: sudden unexplained death of an infant <1 yr. BRUE: brief (<1 min), now-resolved episode of color, breathing, tone or responsiveness change; transport.
One unified 6-link chain for all ages/settings: recognition and emergency activation, high-quality CPR, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-arrest care, recovery and survivorship.
100-120 per minute.
At least 2 inches (5 cm), no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm).

cards.front: Child compression depth (1 yr to puberty)
cards.back: At least 1/3 the AP chest depth, about 2 inches (5 cm). One or two hands.
At least 1/3 the AP chest depth, about 1.5 inches (4 cm).
30:2 for 1 or 2 rescuers (no advanced airway).
2025 AHA: two thumbs (encircling hands) or heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum. The 2-finger technique is no longer recommended.
Two thumb-encircling hands technique on the lower half of the sternum (preferred); heel of one hand if hands cannot encircle the chest.
Heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum (center of chest), other hand on top, arms straight, shoulders over hands.
Allow complete recoil between compressions; do not lean. Leaning reduces venous return.
Minimize interruptions; keep pauses under 10 seconds; chest compression fraction at least 60% (ideally higher).
Switch compressors about every 2 minutes (5 cycles of 30:2) or sooner if fatigued; make the switch in under 5 sec.
At least 5 but no more than 10 seconds. Carotid in adults; carotid or femoral in children; brachial in infants.

cards.front: Rescue breathing rate - adult with pulse
cards.back: 1 breath every 6 seconds (about 10/min), each over 1 sec.
1 breath every 2-3 seconds (20-30/min). If heart rate is <60 with poor perfusion despite oxygen and ventilation, start CPR.

cards.front: Ventilation with advanced airway during CPR
cards.back: Continuous compressions without pausing for breaths. Adult: 1 breath every 6 sec (10/min). Infant/child: 1 every 2-3 sec (20-30/min).

cards.front: Where to place patient for CPR
cards.back: Supine on a firm, flat surface; expose the chest.
For untrained lay rescuers of adults: call 911, push hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100-120/min. Children need breaths too.
Unresponsive, no normal breathing (absent or only gasping), and no definite pulse felt within 10 seconds.
1) Power on 2) Attach pads 3) Analyze (everyone clear, no touching) 4) Shock if advised, then resume CPR immediately.
Anterolateral: right upper chest below the clavicle and left side below the armpit (lateral to the nipple). Alternative: anterior-posterior.
Under 8 yr (about <25 kg): pediatric pads/attenuator if available; if not, use adult pads. Pads must not touch; use front-back if needed.
Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT).
Asystole and PEA (pulseless electrical activity). AED says no shock advised: resume CPR immediately; ALS for further care.
Everyone clear before analysis and shock; move free-flowing oxygen away from the chest; dry the chest; remove medication patches and wipe.
Do not place a pad directly over the device (place it to the side, about 1 inch away); do not delay the shock.
Remove from standing water and quickly wipe the chest dry; do not delay the shock. AED use is OK on snow or a wet surface.
Resume CPR immediately, starting with compressions, for about 2 minutes (5 cycles) before the AED re-analyzes. No pulse check right after the shock.
ROSC, care transferred to ALS/equal or higher level, rescuer exhaustion, unsafe scene, valid DNR/POLST presented, or termination order from medical direction.
Injuries incompatible with life (decapitation, transection, incineration), rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition. Withhold CPR per local protocol.
Return of spontaneous circulation: a palpable pulse returns (breathing may not). Support ventilation, recheck often, transport.
Support airway/ventilation at normal rate (no hyperventilation); titrate O2 once SpO2 is reliable (2025 AHA 90-98%, per protocol); vitals, transport.
No pulse: standard CPR with ventilations and AED take priority; give naloxone per protocol without delaying CPR. Pulse but not breathing: ventilate + naloxone.
Hypoxic arrest: ventilation matters. AHA: open the airway, give 2 rescue breaths, then CPR 30:2 with oxygen; attach AED when available.
Pulse may be slow and weak: check longer than usual (30-60 sec per local protocol). No pulse: CPR and AED, prevent heat loss, transport; shock limits per protocol.
High-quality CPR with continuous manual left uterine displacement if the uterus is at/above the umbilicus; early ALS and rapid transport.
Right atrium > tricuspid > right ventricle > pulmonic valve > lungs > left atrium > mitral > left ventricle > aortic valve > body.
Supply the heart muscle; fill during diastole. Blockage causes ischemia/infarct.
Tachycardia >100 bpm; bradycardia <60 bpm.
Normal is below 120/80 mmHg; hypotension in adults is generally systolic <90 mmHg.
Stroke volume: blood per beat. CO = HR x SV. BP = CO x peripheral resistance.
Preload: volume returning to the heart (filling). Afterload: resistance the ventricle pumps against.
Chest pain from temporary myocardial ischemia, usually on exertion; typically lasts under 15 min and is relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
Stable: predictable on exertion, relieved by rest. Unstable: at rest, increasing, lasts longer; treat as possible MI.
Death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery. Pain often lasts >15-30 min and is not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
Umbrella term: unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI.
Crushing pressure/tightness, radiating to arm/jaw/back, diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea, anxiety, pale/ashen.
Women, elderly, diabetics: fatigue, indigestion, shortness of breath, nausea, weakness with little pain.
Onset, Provocation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, Time - pain assessment.
Signs/symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last oral intake, Events leading up.
Primary assessment, O2 only if hypoxic/dyspneic, position of comfort, vitals, aspirin, assist nitro per protocol, 12-lead acquisition if allowed, early transport.
Suspected ACS/cardiac chest pain. Antiplatelet: keeps platelets from clumping so the clot does not grow.
162-324 mg non-enteric-coated, chewed (2-4 x 81 mg chewable tablets), per local protocol.
Aspirin/NSAID allergy, active GI bleeding or ulcer, bleeding disorder, aspirin-sensitive asthma; full dose already taken. Per local protocol.
Cardiac-type chest pain in a patient with their own prescribed nitro (and protocol/medical direction). Vasodilator: lowers preload and heart workload.
0.4 mg sublingual tablet or spray; may repeat every 3-5 min if pain persists and BP allows, max 3 doses total (including doses already taken).
SBP <100 (<90 in some protocols); PDE5 inhibitor use (sildenafil/vardenafil within 24 h, tadalafil within 48 h); head injury; 3 doses already taken.
Headache, hypotension, dizziness, flushing, burning under the tongue. Recheck BP within 5 min after each dose.
Tablets lose potency with light, heat, air and age (keep in original dark glass bottle); check expiration. Give with patient seated or lying.
Right patient (their own prescription), right drug/dose/route, not expired, SBP above protocol minimum, no PDE5 use, medical direction as required.
Heart cannot pump effectively. Left-sided: pulmonary edema (crackles, dyspnea, orthopnea). Right-sided: JVD, peripheral edema, ascites.
Difficulty breathing lying flat; paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea wakes patient at night; signs of CHF.
Signs of right-sided heart failure: swollen feet/ankles (dependent edema) and distended neck veins.
Pump failure (often after MI): hypotension, cool clammy skin, weak rapid pulse, possible pulmonary edema. O2, position of comfort, rapid transport/ALS.
Beck's triad: hypotension (narrowing pulse pressure), JVD, muffled heart sounds, from blood/fluid in the pericardial sac.
Severely high BP (often >180/120) with organ signs: headache, vision change, chest pain, AMS. Supportive care; do not try to lower BP; transport.
Weakened aortic wall bulges. Rupture: sudden severe abdominal/back pain, pulsating mass, shock. Do not palpate repeatedly; rapid transport.
Sudden tearing/ripping chest or back pain, unequal pulses or BP between arms; time critical, rapid transport.
Tachycardia, bradycardia, VF and pulseless VT (shockable), asystole/PEA (not shockable). EMTs do not interpret ECGs; use AED, call ALS.
ST-elevation MI: usually complete blockage of a coronary artery. Time critical: early hospital notification, transport to PCI-capable center per protocol.
Protein released by injured heart muscle; rises hours after an MI. Measured by hospital lab to confirm MI.
Brief loss of consciousness from reduced brain perfusion with spontaneous recovery. Cardiac causes are serious; assess vitals, glucose; consider ALS.
Plaque build-up in arteries narrowing the lumen; leading cause of MI/stroke.
Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history. Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity, inactivity.
